title: 13 — Java Modular Monolith, Plug-ins and Approval Workflows
html:
13 — Java Modular Monolith, Plug-ins and Approval Workflows

The one idea: an agent runtime is easiest to run as one deployable whose capabilities are plug-in modules loaded in-process — no network hop between "the agent" and "the SQL tool". Spring Boot hosts it, Java's ServiceLoader discovers the plug-ins, OpenFeign and Redis connect it to identity and entitlement services, Flowable enforces four-eyes approval, and Server-Sent Events stream each turn to the browser.

1. Modular monolith — definition

A modular monolith is a single deployable application divided into modules with explicit boundaries: each module owns its code and data, exposes a small public interface, and does not reach into other modules' internals.

Microservices Modular monolith
Deployment Many services One
Calls between modules Network (latency, retries, partial failure) In-process method calls
Boundaries enforced by Network Build rules, package visibility, architecture tests
Operational cost High Low
Independent scaling Per service Whole app (or extract a module later)

For an agent turn that calls five tools, five in-process calls instead of five HTTP calls removes latency and a whole class of failures. Extract a module into a service only when it truly needs separate scaling or ownership. See Architecture styles.

2. Plug-in modules with Java SPI (ServiceLoader)

2.1 How SPI works

  1. Define a service interface in a shared API module.
  2. Each plug-in JAR implements it and registers the implementation in META-INF/services/<fully.qualified.InterfaceName> (a text file with one implementation class per line), or with provides … with … in module-info.java.
  3. At runtime ServiceLoader.load(Interface.class) finds every registered implementation on the class/module path.

Drop a new JAR on the path → a new capability, no change to the core.

2.2 The contract

// agent-api module
package dev.notes.agent.api;

public interface AgentModule {
    String id();                                     // "sql-rag", "document-rag", "graph-rag", …
    Set<Intent> handles();                           // which classified intents it serves
    ToolSchema schema();                             // typed input/output description
    ModuleResult execute(ModuleRequest request, TurnContext ctx);
}

2.3 A plug-in

// sql-rag module
package dev.notes.agent.sqlrag;

public final class SqlRagModule implements AgentModule {
    public String id() { return "sql-rag"; }
    public Set<Intent> handles() { return Set.of(Intent.METRIC_LOOKUP, Intent.COMPARISON); }
    public ToolSchema schema() { return ToolSchema.of(MetricQuery.class, MetricAnswer.class); }

    public ModuleResult execute(ModuleRequest req, TurnContext ctx) {
        MetricQuery q = req.as(MetricQuery.class);
        ctx.entitlements().require("gold.metrics", q.entityId());
        MetricAnswer a = certifiedMetrics.lookup(q, ctx.asOf());        // deterministic, from Gold
        return ModuleResult.of(a).withVintage(a.vintage()).withSource(a.sourceRef());
    }
}

# sql-rag/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/dev.notes.agent.api.AgentModule
dev.notes.agent.sqlrag.SqlRagModule

2.4 Loading into Spring

@Configuration
class ModuleRegistryConfig {
    @Bean
    ModuleRegistry moduleRegistry() {
        Map<String, AgentModule> modules = ServiceLoader.load(AgentModule.class).stream()
            .map(ServiceLoader.Provider::get)
            .collect(Collectors.toMap(AgentModule::id, m -> m));
        return new ModuleRegistry(modules);
    }
}

Typical modules: Document RAG, SQL RAG over Gold views, Graph RAG over the relationship graph, Glossary Normaliser (maps user terms to ontology concepts), Report Builder, Evaluators.

.NET equivalent: loading implementations of an interface from assemblies in a plug-in folder (AssemblyLoadContext + reflection, or MEF).

3. Integration: OpenFeign, Eureka and Redis

3.1 OpenFeign — declarative REST clients

@FeignClient(name = "entitlement-service")          // name resolved through service discovery
interface EntitlementClient {
    @GetMapping("/v1/users/{userId}/entitlements")
    EntitlementSet entitlementsFor(@PathVariable String userId);
}

@SpringBootApplication
@EnableFeignClients
class AgentRuntimeApplication { public static void main(String[] a) { SpringApplication.run(AgentRuntimeApplication.class, a); } }

Add timeouts and a circuit breaker (Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker / Resilience4j) — an entitlement outage must deny, not allow.

3.2 Eureka — service discovery

A registry where services announce themselves; Feign looks up entitlement-service there instead of hard-coding a URL. On Kubernetes you can use its DNS-based discovery instead.

3.3 Redis — caching

@Service
class CachedEntitlements {
    private final EntitlementClient client;
    CachedEntitlements(EntitlementClient client) { this.client = client; }

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "entitlements", key = "#userId")   // short TTL configured on the cache
    public EntitlementSet forUser(String userId) { return client.entitlementsFor(userId); }
}

Cache entitlements briefly (minutes), glossary and schema lookups longer, and never cache an LLM answer across users with different entitlements.

4. Maker-checker with Flowable BPMN

4.1 Four-eyes principle

Any consequential change needs two different people: a maker proposes, a checker approves. Used for certifying a data release to Gold, accepting a restatement, overriding an entity match, or letting an agent perform an action with side effects.

4.2 The process

---
title: Maker-checker certification process
---
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Draft: maker prepares release
    Draft --> Submitted: maker submits with quality card
    Submitted --> UnderReview: checker claims task
    UnderReview --> Approved: checker approves
    UnderReview --> Rejected: checker rejects with reason
    Rejected --> Draft: maker revises
    Approved --> Certified: system tags Iceberg snapshot
    Certified --> [*]

BPMN pieces: a user task for the maker, a user task for the checker restricted to the checkers group, an exclusive gateway on the decision, and a service task that creates the Iceberg tag (vintage_YYYY_MM_DD) and signs it.

4.3 Driving it from Java

@Service
class CertificationWorkflow {
    private final RuntimeService runtime;
    private final TaskService tasks;

    CertificationWorkflow(RuntimeService runtime, TaskService tasks) {
        this.runtime = runtime; this.tasks = tasks;
    }

    String submit(String maker, String table, long snapshotId) {
        return runtime.startProcessInstanceByKey("certifyRelease",
            Map.of("maker", maker, "table", table, "snapshotId", snapshotId)).getId();
    }

    List<Task> pendingFor(String checker) {
        return tasks.createTaskQuery().taskCandidateGroup("checkers").list();
    }

    void decide(String taskId, String checker, boolean approved, String reason) {
        String maker = (String) tasks.getVariable(taskId, "maker");
        if (maker.equals(checker)) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Four-eyes rule: the maker cannot approve their own release");
        }
        tasks.claim(taskId, checker);
        tasks.complete(taskId, Map.of("approved", approved, "checker", checker, "reason", reason));
    }
}

Enforce "maker ≠ checker" in code, not just in the UI; Flowable records who did what and when for audit.

4.4 Cryptographic vintage tag

On approval, the service task:

  1. Creates an Iceberg tag on the approved snapshot, e.g. vintage_2026_10_31.
  2. Computes a digest of (table, snapshot ID, metadata file location, quality card, approvers).
  3. Signs the digest (e.g. with a key in a key vault) and stores the signature with the tag.

Consumers can verify that the data they read is exactly what was approved.

5. The eight-step agent turn, streamed with SSE

5.1 The steps

# Step What happens
1 Receive Authenticate, load conversation, attach user entitlements
2 Classify Intent (metric lookup, comparison, document question, graph question, action request) and risk level
3 Normalise Resolve entity names to canonical IDs, terms to glossary concepts, dates to periods
4 Route Pick modules for the intent; high-risk actions → maker-checker
5 Discover Load the chosen modules' tool schemas (MCP or SPI)
6 Execute Call tools/modules; model composes the answer from tool results and retrieved chunks
7 Check output Every number traceable to a tool result, citations valid, vintage present, no personal data, policy checks
8 Persist Store the turn, tool calls, sources, vintage and trace ID

5.2 Streaming with Server-Sent Events

SSE is a one-way stream over HTTP (text/event-stream). The browser's EventSource reconnects automatically. Ideal for "step 3 of 8 done…" progress and token streaming.

@RestController
class TurnController {
    private final TurnPipeline pipeline;
    TurnController(TurnPipeline pipeline) { this.pipeline = pipeline; }

    @PostMapping(path = "/v1/turns", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    SseEmitter turn(@RequestBody TurnRequest req, @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt user) {
        SseEmitter emitter = new SseEmitter(Duration.ofMinutes(2).toMillis());
        Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> {               // Java 21 virtual threads
            try {
                pipeline.run(req, user, (step, payload) ->
                    emitter.send(SseEmitter.event().name(step).data(payload)));
                emitter.complete();
            } catch (Exception e) {
                emitter.completeWithError(e);
            }
        });
        return emitter;
    }
}

// Browser. EventSource only does GET, so POST the question first, then stream by turn id —
// or use fetch() and read the response body stream.
const es = new EventSource(`/v1/turns/${turnId}/events`);
es.addEventListener("classify", e => showStep("Classified", JSON.parse(e.data)));
es.addEventListener("answer", e => renderAnswer(JSON.parse(e.data)));

The same pattern works in ASP.NET Core (text/event-stream response with IAsyncEnumerable) or FastAPI (StreamingResponse).

6. Questions to test yourself

  1. What does a modular monolith give up compared with microservices, and what does it gain for an agent runtime?
  2. Write the META-INF/services file for two plug-ins implementing AgentModule.
  3. Why must an entitlement-service failure result in denial, and how do you implement that with Feign?
  4. Where is "maker ≠ checker" enforced, and what does Flowable record for audit?
  5. Which of the eight turn steps would block an answer containing a number not returned by any tool?

7. Review checklist

  • Modules communicate through interfaces only; architecture tests enforce boundaries.
  • Plug-ins discovered with ServiceLoader; each declares its intents and schema.
  • Feign clients have timeouts and fail closed; entitlements cached briefly.
  • Certification and risky agent actions go through a BPMN maker-checker process.
  • Certified releases are tagged and signed.
  • Each agent turn runs the eight steps and is persisted with its trace.
